newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Compromise sought by world forum on ivory trade.
newsitem.headline: Compromise sought by world forum on ivory trade.

text.p: A world forum on endangered species, bogged down by a row over the future of the elephant, began a search on Wednesday for a compromise to a controversial proposal by three southern African states to resume trade in ivory.

The 10-day Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) postponed for the second time in 24 hours voting on the proposal by Zimbabwe, Botswana and Namibia, saying many delegates had indicated in overnight consultations they wanted the issue to be thoroughly thrashed by a special working group.
CITES first postponed a vote on the issue on Tuesday after a four-hour debate that went well past the conference closing time.
"The feeling is that maybe some further discussion may produce a compromise," said conference chairman David Brackett, a Canadian.
He said the 19-member working group would report back to the main CITES conference later on Wednesday, but many delegates said it was likely to drag on to Thursday.
The ivory trade and African elephant debate has overshadowed all other issues at the CITES meeting which ends on Friday.
Zimbabwe's Environment and Tourism Minister Chen Chimutengwende said a possible compromise could be worked around an amendment proposed by South Africa but was defeated by a slim margin on Tuesday.
"There is room to work around that," he told Reuters.

South Africa's proposed amendment to ease the ban to allow commercial trade to start only in 1999, with some fixed quotas, was just three votes short of the 78 three-thirds majority it needed from the 123 countries that voted. Forty-one countries voted against the amendment, and seven abstained.
Botswana, Zimbabwe and Namibia argue that limited and strictly supervised trade will not threaten their "excess' elephant herd, now estimated at around 150,000.

They are strongly backed by Japan and Switzerland but face stiff opposition from influential green movements and countries, including the United States and from the European Union, who argue that easing the ban will leave elephants at the mercy of poachers.

The debate has exposed deep divisions across the globe on how countries view the issue -- and the arguments advanced by Zimbabwe over the past week that most of the rich North was against ivory trade and a majority of the poor South for it.
Delegates from some 62 countries participated in the debate on Tuesday, from the United States to Nepal, Switzerland to war-torn Liberia.
Switzerland hit out at the CITES conference, accusing it of shifting goal posts to deny the southern Africans a legitimate right to sustainable utilisation of their natural resources.
